Uses X as a sound selector. Copies six bytes of stream pointers from $0C20 into $03B4-$03B9 and the mode byte from $0C14 into $0495. Clears the voice state and writes the initial volume and envelope registers.
Saved selector added back while calculating the six-byte offset in the order pointer table. The next loop copies the three low and three high bytes.
Current sound selector stored in the immediate operand of the LDA at $043B. The order reader also checks this byte to decide whether to use the title tune's restart pointers.
Sets the update guard at $048E, then clears control and envelope registers for the three voices through $0467.
Returns while the guard at $048E is nonzero. Otherwise it traverses three SID voices using the stream pointers at $03B4 and $03B7.
Setup writes the selected cue's mode into this immediate byte. The update loop then initializes the visit to the voices, sets the register offset and reads the current order.
Reads the next command at the current voice's stream address. $FE halts the driver. $FF resets its counters and, on selection 0, installs replacement stream pointers from $0C68 and $0C6B.
Patched high byte of the order read at $04C9. The interpreter tests incoming bytes for end or restart, then separates pitch, speed and pattern selections by their ranges.
Doubles the order value and reads a little-endian pattern pointer at $0C6E. Handles leading filter commands and commands that set voice parameters before the note.
Copies the duration to the countdown, adds the voice's transposition to the note index, fetches its two frequency bytes from $0B5E and $0BB9, then writes the frequency and envelope for that voice.
Advances the voice pattern index past the filter setting. Stores the next pattern byte for further decoding unless it is the end command.
Uses eight-byte instrument records. Loads the last three fields into $E1–$E3 and tests the flags to select later waveform and pitch calculations.
Patched high byte of the indexed read at $0719. The loaded byte is added to the note index before fetching its frequency word.
The code rewrites the first opcode here from the high bit of $E1. Changes whether this pass adds or subtracts the note-spacing term before writing the pitch.
Instrument-specific limit patched into the CMP at $07C8. The note age controls whether the loop subtracts another pitch increment.
Immediate operand read after pulling the shifted note-step calculation. The path measures the distance between the current note and its stored target using both pitch tables.
Part of the slide calculation that adds each fractional step, shifts its two-byte result and patches the later pitch update.
The immediate of the ADC at $08C5. The path writes the adjusted high frequency, or reloads the note target and clears slide state, then checks the voice's instrument for further changes.
In the selector 6 trace, the voice reads this profile to set the filter mode and select a cutoff change by the voice's age.
Advances into later age boundaries in the waveform table. Branches select a signed step and update the voice's current stage according to its age.
Patched high-byte ceiling compared after stepping the pulse. The next path increments or decrements the two-byte state and checks another profile bound.
Immediate gate setting read on the timed waveform path. The surrounding code uses the selected profile to keep or reset waveform state and sets up the optional filter path.
Low part of the indirect filter profile address. The path reads the mode and decides which cutoff entry to use by comparing the voice age with profile boundaries.
Starts with bytes read indirectly by $0551 and its continuation in the selector 1 test. These are pattern data addressed by the pointer table, despite residing amid the driver routines.
Converts a selected time entry to its delta position in the filter profile. Adds the delta to that voice's stored cutoff and routes the result to the cutoff register.
High byte of the load at $0A88. The loaded control value sets the voice's waveform and contributes to the following gate mask.
High byte of the pitch-profile fetch at $0A9C. The effect uses the byte as either a relative note adjustment or part of an absolute pitch write.
Pattern bytes read by the three-voice title/ending selection. $0551 reads its first token and its continuation at $06A7 or $0663 reads later values.
In this profile path uses the profile byte as the high frequency and sets the low frequency to zero, then writes the voice registers via $0B24.
Patched operand used before restoring the stored pitch and waveform for a voice. The continuation masks its control byte and writes it to the active SID channel.
Low bytes of the SID frequency values, indexed by note after adding the voice transposition.
The same low-byte frequency table seen from its second byte. The note-spacing routine subtracts the current note's low byte from this next note.
Tail of the low-byte frequency table, indices $41 through $5A. The next voice pitch fetch uses the same index for the corresponding high byte.
High bytes paired with $0B5E. A change of pitch can read both tables again without starting a fresh note.
The next note's high byte for the same subtraction after the low bytes have set carry.
Tail of the matching high-frequency byte table, also indexed from $41 through $5A.

Jumps to the new-game setup at $2C11. The following bytes starting at $2C03 are mutable gameplay state.
An index below $80 requests a new SID selection. The update routine at $2E8D consumes it and replaces it with $80.
Current level resource index. Setup at $2C11 begins at zero. The transition at $63B7 uses 0 through 5 as the disk selector and sends 6 to the ending path.
Resets the resource index, takes the title's selection from $1A63 minus one into $2F0A, calls common score and life setup, then falls through to level setup.

Resets the level's gameplay state, copies the initial actor sprite pointers, sets up video and the level initialisation calls, then installs the hardware IRQ at $2D5E and enters the main loop at $5FE5. The disk transition at $63C2 enters here without resetting the resource index.
Saves A, Y and X and acknowledges the VIC interrupt. Dispatches the four states 0 to 3 from zero-page $34 to $308E, $319C, $3252 or $32C0; other values take the longer update starting at $2D8F.
The first raster-change case jumps to $308E, which writes the lower-half sprite positions and pointers. The next three jump stubs handle the other positions in sorted order.

Updates scrolling and sprite setup, advances player recovery or action states, and polls a port when its actor is ready. The active-player mode gates each actor's calls. The routine then checks the camera constraints, player contact and pending sound.
When $2C04 is nonnegative, starts that sound through $040E and then writes $80 to mark the request handled. On the negative path calls the regular SID update at $048D instead.
Four vertical positions. The drawing order compares these at $2F22, and the first set of sprite layers uses them as the VIC Y coordinates.
Four actor indices sorted by vertical position at $2F11. Adjacent entries with equal Y keep their order.
Four bytes per actor in sixteen bytes. The first two give the overlaid shapes above the waist and the second two give the shapes below it.
Low eight bits of four actor X positions. Port 2's right branch increments the first actor's value twice, subject to movement checks.
Zero after moving left through $350A, one after moving right through $35A4. The fire dispatcher reads this to choose between two direction dispatches.
Attack or movement state for the first actor. $4417 doubles it to select a routine from the little-endian jump table starting at $442B.
Port 1's fire dispatcher stores the second actor's state here. For example, $4B15 stores $01 for left and fire when the second actor faces left.
The update distinguishes 0 (first player only), 1 (both players) and 2 (second player only). The first or second player leaving play can change mode 1 to 2 or 0 respectively.
Sorts four actor indices by nondecreasing Y, then copies each actor's four sprite pointers into $24–$33 and two colour values into $35–$3C in that order.

Schedules each upper-to-lower sprite change at actor Y plus 19, capped at $D5. Holds the new sprite Y two lines below that scheduled time. Later comparisons adjust the schedule when changes are close together.

Places four sprite pairs at the sorted actor coordinates. Each pair uses matching X and Y and writes pointers in both graphics screen buffers. Separate pointer pairs are installed during the raster changes.
Writes a common Y to sprites 0 and 1, a common X from $2EEC,Y, and the pair of shape pointers at $30 and $31 to both screen buffers.
Increments the end wait counter. At count $64 sets the flag to return to the title. Sets both players' low X coordinate to 2 on each pass.
Calls both enemy contact routines while the end flags are clear. Otherwise it counts the delayed exit for the corresponding actor.

Reads CIA 1 port A for joystick 2. Tests fire before the direction comparisons when $344E is clear; otherwise advances the counter at $421A and clears the gate at $1B. The direction comparisons dispatch the selected direction or diagonal.
Reads a character from the patched first-player row and uses the level and scrolling position to pick the first tile property table.
High byte patched by the level and camera position. The lookup uses the tile code's high five bits for the table byte and low three for the bit.
High bytes paired with the low bytes at $38A0. The selected pair depends on resource index and, for the first two scenes, the camera column.
High bytes for the second packed property tables. The movement probes use them with the first bytes at $38B8.
Uses the current screen buffer and the second property table for the first player. It patches the row and mask loads to address the correct tile and table.
High address byte of the patched first-player screen row read in the second property test. The read gives the tile code used for the mask.
High byte of the patched address at $394A, which looks up the byte of the first player's second tile property table.
The high address byte of each row in the first display buffer. The lookup doubles the row number and reads this table and $396F together.
The high address byte of each row in the second display buffer, paired with the low byte at $39B3.
Starts looking for a return position when the recovery counter reaches $4B. Holds the counter at $4A while the chosen display row is tested.
Final byte of the patched absolute indexed load for the first player's return scan. When it finds a suitable tile, the code computes an X from the column and clears the recovery counter.
Counts the corresponding recovery wait, uses the row state at $2C07 and prepares the second actor's placement scan.
High byte of the indexed map fetch at $3AA6, patched from the row pointer table. The scan tests columns 12 through 25 and uses the first eligible tile to compute the second player's X and Y.

Reads CIA 1 port B for joystick 1. Tests fire before the direction comparisons when $344F is clear; otherwise advances the counter at $421B and clears the gate at $1B. The direction comparisons dispatch the selected direction or diagonal.
Takes the second player's Y or the probe override. Translates the position to a tile in the current screen buffer and uses the first mask set.
Reads the candidate character from the patched second-player row and selects the first tile property table used for that level.
High byte of the patched address at $4030. The following bit test uses the low three tile bits to choose from the table byte.
Reads the second player's X and Y or the movement overrides. Selects the second per-level tile property table before returning the sampled bit.
High byte of the second player's patched screen-row read. Supplies the character code for the second property table.

High byte of the table address in the LDA at $40CF. The level and two camera column thresholds select a tile collision mask table. The high five bits of the tile code index it and the low three choose its bit.
Starts the fire gate. On level resource 3 it checks four background tile IDs before dispatching. For eligible positions, it checks the facing byte and one of nine port-2 direction and fire values.
Patched high byte of the stage L3 screen read at $426C. The following code refuses the four special tiles $50–$53 before choosing a facing dispatcher.
Clears the attack counter at $2F03 and compares the port with neutral fire or one of eight directions. The handlers select action IDs, with some choices consulting the weapon variable at $2F00.

Compares the same nine port-2 values as the left-facing dispatcher. The branches choose right-facing attack states. Both facings use $12 for up-right and $11 for up-left, and preserve the actor's initial Y for those jumps.

Sets a scroll request when player one's on-screen X reaches $F5. The level and the indexed camera limit decide whether the viewport can continue right. In two-player play the other actor's position can constrain it.

Selects L2's camera bound from $5349. In one-player mode the first fighter can request rightward camera movement without an X check on the absent actor.
Chooses a goal camera column from $5393. While the camera is short of that goal, a second actor left of $84 can hold the scroll.
